exam: A 28‑year‑old at 32 weeks presents with new‑onset hypertension and 1+ proteinuria – what is the immediate management and why? — Diagnose pre‑eclampsia; start antihypertensive if BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg, give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, plan delivery after stabilization.

A woman in labor has sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding – how do you distinguish placental abruption from placenta previa at the bedside? — Abruption: painful uterus, tender, rigid; previa: painless bleeding, soft uterus; speculum exam helps identify source.

Fundal height is 4 cm behind dates at 28 weeks in a malaria‑endemic area – what investigations and steps are appropriate? — Measure blood pressure, urine protein, perform malaria smear, assess fetal growth with ultrasound if possible; treat malaria, monitor fetal well‑being, consider early delivery if severe.

Why is magnesium sulfate preferred over diazepam for seizure prophylaxis in pre‑eclampsia? — Magnesium stabilises neuronal membranes and reduces vasospasm; diazepam does not address underlying endothelial dysfunction and has higher respiratory depression risk.

A patient with known sickle cell disease presents at 30 weeks with hypertension and proteinuria – how does sickle cell affect placental pathology? — Sickle cell can cause vaso‑occlusive infarcts in the placenta, worsening uteroplacental insufficiency and raising pre‑eclampsia risk.

In a setting without Doppler ultrasound, how can you monitor a pregnancy complicated by suspected uteroplacental insufficiency? — Serial fundal height measurements, maternal blood pressure, urine protein, and fetal heart rate monitoring; refer for delivery if growth falters or maternal signs worsen.
ai.title: Placental Development and Disorders
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Placental formation is a stepwise process that determines fetal growth and maternal health. Abnormal placentation underlies many obstetric emergencies, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Implantation: blastocyst adheres to decidua basalis
Cytotrophoblast proliferates → syncytiotrophoblast covers chorionic villi
Spiral arteries remodel to low‑resistance high‑flow vessels
sections.p: The placenta forms from the trophoblast after implantation, establishing maternal‑fetal circulation. Normal stages are implantation, villous formation, and maturation by 12 weeks.

b: Insufficient spiral artery conversion → high‑resistance flow
Excessive trophoblast invasion → placenta previa or accreta spectrum
Maternal infections (malaria, HIV) impair villous development
sections.p: Clinicians must recognise how abnormal remodeling leads to pre‑eclampsia, fetal growth restriction (FGR), and placental abruption.

Fundal height lagging >2 cm behind dates → consider FGR

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, limited imaging makes bedside assessment crucial for detecting placental disorders.

FGR: serial fundal measurements, Doppler if possible, consider early delivery if Doppler shows absent end‑diastolic flow
